Set $\mathcal A=\{a\in E:\operatorname*{ess\,inf}(1+a)>m,\ \operatorname*{ess\,sup}(1+a)<M\}$ and $\sigma=1+a$. Choose an orthonormal spherical-harmonic basis $Y_{\ell k}$ of mean-zero $L^2(S^2)$, with $\ell\ge1$ and $1\le k\le2\ell+1$. For each basis current there is a unique weak solution $u_{\sigma,\ell k}\in H^1(\Omega)$ with boundary mean zero such that
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla v}=\int_{S^2}Y_{\ell k}\overline{\operatorname{Tr}v}\qquad(v\in H^1(\Omega)).$$
The centered sequence
$$G(a):=\big(\operatorname{Tr}(u_{\sigma,\ell k}-u_{1,\ell k})\big)_{\ell,k}$$
belongs to $Y=\ell^2(L^2(S^2))$. The map $G:\mathcal A\to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable, and both $G$ and $G'$ are Lipschitz on $\mathcal A$, with constants depending only on $m,M,\rho$ and the ball. Its derivative in direction $h\in E$ is the trace sequence of the unique boundary-mean-zero solutions
$$\int_\Omega\sigma\nabla v_{h,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla w}=-\int_\Omega h\nabla u_{\sigma,\ell k}\cdot\overline{\nabla w}.$$
The uncentered sequence $(\operatorname{Tr}u_{1,\ell k})_{\ell,k}$ does not belong to $Y$. Thus absolute voltage data in this convention lie in an affine translate of $Y$, whereas data differences belong to $Y$. All complex spaces here may be regarded as real Banach spaces when taking derivatives with respect to real conductivities.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

For its elements, zero extension is bounded into $H^{s_1}(\mathbb R^3)$ by [F3]. Fourier Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|a\|_\infty\le C\|a\|_V$ because $s_1>3/2$. Thus $V$ embeds continuously into the bounded collared coefficient space. The set $\mathcal C-\sigma_0$ is convex and closed in $V$: convexity preserves the pointwise bounds, and uniform convergence from this embedding preserves them under a norm limit.

Choose a smooth scalar function $\vartheta$ with $0\le\vartheta\le1$, equal to one on $[m,M]$ and zero outside $(m/2,2M)$, and set $g(t)=1+\int_1^t\vartheta(u)du$. Then $g(t)=t$ on $[m,M]$, $g(1)=1$, and $m/2\le g(t)\le2M$ globally. All its first and second derivatives are bounded. Put $b(a):=g(\sigma_0+a)-1$. Since $\sigma_0+a=1$ outside $B_\rho$ and $g(1)=1$, $b(a)\in E$ for every $a\in V$. Moreover, $a\mapsto b(a)$ is globally Lipschitz from $V$ into $E$ and continuously Fréchet differentiable, with derivative $b'(a)h=g'(\sigma_0+a)h$ and globally Lipschitz derivative; its Taylor remainder is bounded by $\frac12\|g''\|_\infty\|h\|_\infty^2$.

Use the centered map [F1] with fixed strict ellipticity bounds $m_*:=m/4$ and $M_*:=4M$, and denote it by $G_{m_*,M_*}$. Since $m_*<m/2\le1+b(a)\le2M<M_*$, every $b(a)$ is admissible for that map. Define explicitly
$$\Gamma(a):=G_{m_*,M_*}(b(a))=G_{m_*,M_*}\bigl(g(\sigma_0+a)-1\bigr)\qquad(a\in V).$$
The chain rule gives $\Gamma'(a)h=G'_{m_*,M_*}(b(a))[g'(\sigma_0+a)h]$. The bounded and Lipschitz derivatives of $b$ and the Lipschitz derivative of the centered supplier give all the asserted global bounds for $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$. For $\sigma_0+a\in\mathcal C$, $g(\sigma_0+a)=\sigma_0+a$, so this formula agrees with the centered physical observation.

The identities for $K,r,F$ and the inverse follow by direct substitution. The map $T$ is globally Lipschitz with $L_T\le\operatorname{Lip}(\Gamma)+\|\Gamma'(0)\|$, so both $r$ and $r^{-1}$ have Lipschitz constant at most $1+L_T$ in the sum norm. In particular $\|Pr^{-1}(a,b)-Pr^{-1}(a',b')\|\le(1+L_T)\|(a,b)-(a',b')\|$. The restriction of a bijection to $U$ is a bijection onto $r(U)$; its projected inverse point has the same coefficient and zero artificial voltage, hence remains in $U\cap X_0$. The extension to all of $D=X$ supplies the global factorization domain required by the original generic hypotheses without changing the physical forward map on any admitted point.

The indicator of the convex set in step 1.1 is convex, and adding the quadratic functional makes $\check R$ proper and nonnegative. For any admitted $a$, expansion of its square gives $\check R(a)-\check R(a^\dagger)-\xi^\dagger(a-a^\dagger)=\frac12\|a-a^\dagger\|_V^2$; outside the set the subgradient inequality is automatic because the left value is infinite. This proves the asserted subgradient and exact Bregman formula. On a fixed sublevel $\check R(a)\le R_0$, the coefficients have bounded intrinsic $H^{s_1}$ norm; subtracting the constant background and zero-extending gives a uniform whole-space bound by [F3]. Thus [F2] applies uniformly on that sublevel, including the truth. Applying [F3] yields the VSC source term $C[\log(1/\|\Gamma(a)-\Gamma(a^\dagger)\|)]^{-\nu}$ for small data differences. Replacing the norm argument by its square changes only a fixed constant in the logarithm. Choose $u_0$ small enough and then enlarge $C$ to dominate the source inequality also at larger data differences; on the fixed sublevel the absolute linear pairing is uniformly bounded. The truncated logarithmic index in [F4] is then a valid concave VSC index on the entire sublevel.

Concavity and $\psi(0)=0$ imply subadditivity: for positive $a+b$, $\psi(a)\ge a\psi(a+b)/(a+b)$ and $\psi(b)\ge b\psi(a+b)/(a+b)$; summing gives $\psi(a+b)\le\psi(a)+\psi(b)$. Hence $C_\psi=1$. The derivative remainder of $r$ has only the second component $\Gamma(a_1)-\Gamma(a_2)-\Gamma'(a_2)(a_1-a_2)$. Integrating the Lipschitz derivative along the segment gives norm at most $L\|a_1-a_2\|_V^2/2$. Since $\|a_i\|<R$ and the first component of $r(x_1)-r(x_2)$ is $a_1-a_2$, this is at most $LR\|r(x_1)-r(x_2)\|_Z$. No differentiability of the boundary of $\mathcal C$ is needed, since the map was differentiated on the full ambient space.

If $\widehat r=r(a,z)\in r(U)$, then $\|\widehat r-r(a^\dagger,0)\|_Z\le(1+L_T)\|a-a^\dagger\|_V+\|z\|_Y$. Squaring gives a bound by $4(1+L_T)^2D_{\check R}^{\xi^\dagger}(a,a^\dagger)+2\|z\|_Y^2$. Because $\|z\|<R$, concavity gives $\psi(C_P\|z\|^2)\ge(\|z\|^2/R^2)\psi(C_PR^2)$. The displayed $\widetilde C_Q$ therefore proves the full frozen compatibility inequality for every admitted range variable. Its denominator is positive since the logarithmic index is positive away from zero. The stated $R_P$ has the required lower bound with equality and vanishes at zero.

All projected coefficients in $U$ have $\|\sigma_0+a\|_{s_1,\Omega}\le\|\sigma_0\|_{s_1,\Omega}+R$, so one fixed $R_0$ covers their regularizer values and the truth. The preceding steps verify every structural range, domain, Lipschitz, projection, subgradient, VSC, compatibility and penalty hypothesis. With $p=2$ and $C_\psi=1$, the frozen constants are $t=1/4-2c_{\rm tcr}^2$, $v=3c_{\rm tcr}^2$, $\lambda=1/2$ and $\overline C=4$. The bound $c_{\rm tcr}<1/\sqrt{20}$ makes $t>0$ and $q=v/t<1$. Join this negative-side series to the original curve for $t\ge0$; matching all one-sided derivatives makes the join smooth. Repeat with the reversed parameter at $b$. The nonzero endpoint derivatives persist after shrinking the two extensions. They remain embedded: within each endpoint chart a coordinate with nonzero tangent derivative is strictly monotone; the endpoint image is separated from the compact remainder of the original curve, and the two distinct endpoint neighborhoods can be made disjoint. Thus $\beta$ extends to an embedded open interval containing $J$.

For each transverse jet coefficient $T_{i,\alpha}(s)$ in the chosen endpoint chart, extend that scalar coefficient by the same endpoint Borel construction, using its derivatives $\partial_s^jT_{i,\alpha}$ and a dyadic radius $r_{j,i,\alpha}$. For fixed $j,i,\alpha$, the finitely many derivative bounds of order $m<j$ guarantee a radius because the relevant terms scale as $r^{j-m}$; choose the largest admissible dyadic radius. This preserves compatibility across the extended curve without requiring independently chosen extensions to satisfy new overlap identities. The construction is deterministic for the countable coefficient family and uses no choice axiom.

For the extended curve the normal exponential map $E(s,y)=\exp_{\beta(s)}y$ maps its normal bundle into $X$. Its derivative at $(s,0)$ sends the parameter direction to $\dot\beta(s)$ and is the identity on the normal directions, hence is an isomorphism by [F1] and [F2]. The inverse function theorem gives open local tube charts, including at the original endpoints. A uniform tube over a slightly larger compact interval exists: if injectivity failed at every shrinking radius, compactness would give two collisions converging to zero-section points, which embeddedness identifies; one local inverse chart then excludes them. In one tube chart write the extended prescribed transverse Taylor series as $\sum_{k\ge0}P_k(s,y)$, with $P_k$ homogeneous of degree $k$ in $y$. Fix a smooth transverse cutoff equal to one near zero. This proves the entire finite-union assertion and its parameter-uniform form.

Work with smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere; a knot is a one-component oriented link. A **finite planar code for an oriented knot diagram** consists of finite vertex and edge sets, incidence data, a cyclic order of the four half-edges at every crossing vertex, a pairing of opposite half-edges into the two local branches, an orientation of each edge, and a choice of which branch is over at each crossing. Every other vertex is a bend vertex of valence two. The code includes a finite plane-drawing certificate: rational coordinates for the vertices and bends, and a finite polygonal path for every edge. The certificate must realize the incidences and cyclic orders, have no edge self-intersection, and have pairwise disjoint edge interiors except at the specified bend and crossing vertices; at a crossing the two branches must be transverse. These conditions are checked by finitely many exact segment-intersection tests. Edge orientations must join coherently across each paired branch and each bend vertex, and following the edges through the crossing pairings and the degree-two bend vertices must give one oriented circle. Thus an admissible code represents a connected regular oriented diagram of a single knot. If there are no crossing vertices, the code is one oriented polygonal circle and has one arc. Smooth each bend in a small disk disjoint from all crossings and other edges; the resulting smooth diagram has the same crossing data.

An **under-arc** is a maximal portion of the oriented circle between consecutive points where the knot passes under at a crossing; the over branch is not cut. With no crossings the entire circle is the unique under-arc. A **positive meridian** of an oriented branch is the oriented boundary of a small normal disk, with disk orientation chosen so that the oriented tangent to the branch followed by the disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation of $S^3$. Planarity, incidence, orientation consistency, one-component tracing and the over/under data are input validity conditions; a procedure receiving an invalid finite record must report invalid input rather than repair it. The code stores no algebraic crossing sign: the oriented plane and the direction of the over branch determine which incident under branch is on its left and which is on its right.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be the image of a compact smooth embedded circle, and let $E:N^\perp K\to\mathbb R^3$ be the Euclidean normal-addition map $E(p,v)=p+v$. There is a real $\varepsilon>0$ such that $E$ restricts to a diffeomorphism from $\{(p,v):\|v\|<\varepsilon\}$ onto an open neighborhood $N_\varepsilon$ of $K$. Moreover, $\mathbb R^3\setminus K$ strongly deformation retracts onto $\mathbb R^3\setminus N_\varepsilon$ by pushing each nonzero normal vector radially to length $\varepsilon$. The construction uses only a finite cover of the compact circle and no choice axiom.

If $A\subset X$ is a CW subcomplex and its inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, then $X$ strongly deformation retracts onto $A$. Moreover, if $(Y,B)$ is a CW pair and $u_0,u_1:B\to Z$ are homotopic, then the adjunction spaces $Z\cup_{u_0}Y$ and $Z\cup_{u_1}Y$ are homotopy equivalent relative to their common subspace $Z$.

Let $(X,A)$ be a CW pair with $A\ne\varnothing$ and supplied characteristic maps. The ordinary quotient $X/A$ is a CW complex, with one vertex $*$ replacing $A$ and one cell of the same dimension for every cell of $X\setminus A$.

If $A$ admits a contraction $H:A\times I\to A$, $H(-,0)=\mathrm{id}_A$, $H(-,1)=a\in A$, then the quotient map $q:X\to X/A$ is a homotopy equivalence and a weak homotopy equivalence. If $H(a,t)=a$ for every $t$, the constructed inverse and inverse homotopies are based at $a$ and $*$. No choice principle is required; a contraction is one witness, not a family of selected contractions.

If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].

Let $Q=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be pointed at $[0]$, and for $r\in\mathbb N$ put

$$W_r:=\bigvee_{j<r}(Q,[0]).$$

Then $\pi_1(W_r,w)$ is the free group on the $r$ standard loops, one traversing each circle summand once. In particular it has rank $r$ ([[def-rank-of-a-finite-rank-free-group]]). For $r=0$, $W_0$ is a point and the basis is empty.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

derivations.claim: Cut out disjoint small underpass intervals, one in each crossing box. The remaining projected arcs are embedded and pairwise disjoint: an interior double point would have an underpassing preimage, which has been removed. Put these arcs at height $1$, their ends in the plane $z=0$, and join each pair of ends of a removed underpass below that plane. This normalization preserves the complement pair. Indeed, inside a crossing box the two branches retain a strict height inequality while their heights interpolate; away from these boxes projection is injective and vertical interpolation cannot introduce intersections. A change of height $d(q)$ on a strand extends to a local ambient map $(q,z)\mapsto(q,z+\chi(z)d(q))$, subdividing the interpolation so that $1+\chi'(z)d(q)>0$. Finitely many disjoint strip charts, smooth cutoffs and parameter subdivisions suffice. Planar bends can likewise be straightened in their disjoint strip charts. All these maps are the identity in a common high collar.

For $c=0$, first compare the actual smooth knot with a polygon, rather than identifying embeddings merely from the code. Its projection is a smooth embedded circle $\gamma$, so the knot is $(\gamma(s),g(s))$. Apply the finite compact-tube construction [F2] to the flat curve $(\gamma(s),0)$: the planar slice of its normal tube is an injective strip $\Psi(s,r)=\gamma(s)+r n(s)$, with $n$ the positive unit planar normal. In this strip the ambient map $(\Psi(s,r),z)\mapsto(\Psi(s,r),z-t\chi(r)g(s))$, with $\chi(0)=1$ and $\chi$ zero near the strip boundary, is a homeomorphism for each $t$ (it is a translation on every vertical fibre), and is the identity outside the strip. It flattens the actual knot. Uniform continuity of the tangent and the finite tube bounds then give a sufficiently fine inscribed polygon: each chord stays in the strip and its projection to the circle is strictly increasing, since its tangent has positive scalar product with the nearby oriented circle tangents. The polygonal projection has one full turn, so it is bijective, and the polygon is the normal graph $r=f(s)$. Choose the subdivision so $\|f\|_\infty\|\chi'\|_\infty<1$. The fibre maps $r\mapsto r+t\chi(r)f(s)$ are strictly increasing homeomorphisms fixing the strip boundary; extended by the identity, they give an ambient planar isotopy carrying $\gamma$ to this polygon. Its product with the identity in $z$ is an ambient three-dimensional isotopy. All subdivisions and bounds use a finite cover and one sufficiently large subdivision number. This relates the actual embedding to the polygon without any later diagram-code supplier.

Here is a precise convenient tunnel model for the normalized knot. In each crossing box choose a small convex polygonal footprint $F_i$ and a convex lower cap $C_i=\{(q,z):q\in F_i,\ h_i(q)\le z\le0\},$ where $h_i$ is piecewise linear, negative inside $F_i$ and zero on its boundary. Take the lower arc to be the two straight segments from its two interior top-face endpoints to one interior point of $C_i$. This replacement of the underpass is realized by vertical interpolation of its negative graph, fixing its endpoints. Each $C_i$ is a product neighborhood of that arc: radial coordinates from the interior vertex identify $C_i$ with a ball; on its boundary send two disjoint disks around the endpoints of a diameter to small disks around the two top endpoints, and extend radially. Such a boundary map is constructed by joining the disk centers by simple polygonal arcs, taking rectangular strips around those arcs, and using affine maps on a finite common triangulation; outside the strips it is the identity. Thus it identifies a standard cylinder core with the two-segment arc and its two end disks with the designated exits. Attach product tubes along the disjoint upper arcs to those exits. The resulting neighborhood $N_*$ has one cap and one upper tube per underpass, joined in the same single cycle as $K$; its coordinates are a disk bundle around $K$, not an assumption about an arbitrary regular neighborhood. Corners and the core bends can be rounded inside disjoint smaller charts; retain the polygonal cap boundary, which is only used topologically.

The polygon's bounded side is supplied by [F6]. Triangulate it by diagonals: at a convex vertex use its neighbor triangle if it contains no other vertex; otherwise join it to a vertex in that triangle farthest from the opposite side. The smaller open triangle contains no intervening vertex, so the diagonal is internal; induction on the vertex count yields a finite triangulation. A leaf of its triangle-adjacency tree is an ear $uvw$, with ear tip $v$ and base $uw$. Remove any collinear vertices before this step. Put $q$ in the interior of $uw$. Choose $z_+=q+(1+\eta)(v-q)$ and $z_-=q-\epsilon(v-q)$, with small positive $\eta,\epsilon$, so the convex quadrilateral $Q=(u,z_+,w,z_-)$ meets the rest of the polygon only at $u,w$. Such bounds exist because the closed ear has no other polygon points, nonadjacent edges have positive separation, and the two remaining incident edges have a positive angle away from the ear; finite determinant and distance comparisons select the bounds. Both $v$ and $q$ are interior to $Q$. Triangulate $Q$ by the fan from $v$. On each fan triangle map its apex $v$ to $v_t=(1-t)v+tq$, fix its two boundary vertices, and interpolate affinely. Since $Q$ is convex and $v_t$ is always interior, the image triangles are a nondegenerate fan partition of the same quadrilateral. The resulting map is therefore injective, surjective and piecewise linear, fixes the whole boundary, and extends by the identity to an ambient plane isotopy. At $t=1$ it sends the two ear edges $uv,vw$ onto $uq,qw$, while fixing all other polygon edges. This is an ambient straightening, not a collapse of a triangle to its base. Inductively remove the ears until a triangle remains. From an interior point of that triangle its boundary has a continuous positive radial-distance function $R(\theta)$; the plane homeomorphism multiplying each ray's radius by $1/R(\theta)$ sends it to a round circle. The products of these plane maps with the identity in $z$ identify the actual knot complement with the round-circle complement.

The model can be compared with the given sufficiently small normal tube without invoking a uniqueness theorem or choice. Make its disk-bundle chart smooth near the core and normalize its differential there to the given normal chart; the required linear change is fibrewise, with the tangential component removed by a change of core parameter. In finitely many charts the two resulting embeddings differ by $O(|v|^2)$, with derivative difference $O(|v|)$. Replace the model chart near $v=0$ by the given one using a radial cutoff supported where $|v|<2\delta$ and equal to one for $|v|\le\delta$. The derivative of the correction is $O(\delta)$; compactness and a finite minimum of the chart injectivity bounds therefore preserve a bundle embedding for small $\delta$. Injectivity between nonadjacent core charts follows from their positive separation. The modified chart equals the given normal chart for $|v|\le\delta$ and retains $N_*$ as its outer boundary. Choose the normal-tube radius $\rho<\delta$. In these product coordinates, replace every fibre radius $r\in[\rho,1]$ by $(1-s)r+s$ and fix the exterior of $N_*$. This is a strong deformation retraction from $E_K$ to $\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N_*$, fixed on its target. It agrees on the outer boundary and never enters the removed radius-$\rho$ tube.

Take a large ball $B_R$ containing $N_*$. Outside it, the homotopy $x\mapsto((1-s)+sR/|x|)x$, with the interior fixed, retracts the exterior to its truncation $X$ in $B_R$. Its outer sphere is retained. Write $A=X\cap\{z\ge0\}$. Below the plane, the exterior is exactly $B=\{(q,z):-\sqrt{R^2-|q|^2}\le z\le h(q)\},$ where $h=h_i$ on $F_i$ and is zero elsewhere; enlarge $R$ so every cap lies above the lower hemisphere. The top plates of the caps belong to $A$ as tube-boundary faces, except for the two exits occupied by upper tubes. Thus $X=A\cup B$ and $A\cap B$ is the equatorial disk with the interiors of the $F_i$ removed. On $B$ use $(q,z)\mapsto(q,(1-s)z+s h(q))$ and on $A$ the identity. These maps agree on the overlap, remain in the indicated vertical intervals, and paste continuously because the two sets are closed in $X$. They fix their target $Y_*=A\cup\bigcup_i D_i,\qquad D_i=\{(q,h_i(q)):q\in F_i\},$ pointwise. This proves the global strong deformation retraction, including the lower region and infinity.

The upper region $A$ is a ball with the neighborhoods of $c$ disjoint boundary-parallel arcs removed. The parallelism disks are the vertical curtains beneath their disjoint projected arcs. Their strip neighborhoods are disjoint. Cutting these strips off the upper half-ball leaves a ball with finitely many boundary indentations: flatten each indentation in its rectangular strip coordinate, fixing the other faces. The strip containing an arc is a ball with a straight diameter tube removed. In cylindrical coordinates this last space is $S^1\times\{(r,z):r\ge\epsilon,\ r^2+z^2\le1\},$ whose second factor is a convex disk. Hence $A$ is a boundary connected sum of $c$ solid tori, glued through specified disks to the remaining ball. For an actual bouquet spine, cut each solid torus across a meridian disk and absorb its remaining ball into the central ball. The result is a central ball with $c$ product one-handles. Join the centers of the $2c$ attaching disks to an interior point by disjoint star arms in that ball; after flattening the finitely many boundary disks, these are radial arms from their centers to the central point. Add the one-handle core intervals. The resulting embedded graph is a bouquet of $c$ circles, since every vertex other than the central one has degree two.

To specify the CW structure for the relative contraction, use a finite polyhedral ball model for the central ball. Triangulate its boundary so that each attaching disk is a subcomplex and its center is a vertex, then cone that boundary triangulation to one interior vertex. Each radial star arm is an edge of this cone triangulation. The union $C$ of the attaching disks and these star edges is a finite CW subcomplex. It is contractible by contracting each disk to its center and then the star to the interior vertex. The central ball $B_0$ and $C$ are both nonempty and contractible, so the inclusion $C\hookrightarrow B_0$ is a homotopy equivalence. By [F3], $B_0$ strongly deformation retracts onto $C$, fixing $C$ pointwise; HEP alone is not being used to assert a contraction. Next contract every attaching disk linearly to its center, and contract the transverse disk factor of each product one-handle by the same linear factor. These formulas agree on the end disks and fix the star edges and handle cores, so they paste to a strong deformation retraction onto the stated bouquet.

For each drilled arc, orient its graph loop to represent the based positive meridian. In an oriented normal-disk chart along the oriented knot tangent, choose the disk orientation so that tangent followed by disk orientation agrees with the ambient orientation, and traverse the disk boundary in its induced positive direction. In the complement product $S^1\times D^2$ of the drilled tube, this boundary is the $S^1$ factor; contracting the disk factor and using the retained collar access path carries it to the corresponding bouquet loop. Thus the chosen generator is the positive meridian, not its inverse. Each such loop crosses precisely its own curtain once. Consequently [F5] identifies these positively oriented meridians as the free basis, rather than merely normal generators.

Fix disk coordinates $\phi_i:\overline D^2\to D_i$ and constants $0<r_0<r_1<1$. In $Y_*$ set $V_i=\phi_i(\{|v|<r_1\})$ and let $U$ be the complement of the union of the closed disks $\phi_i(\{|v|\le r_0\})$. These sets are relative-open: the cap interiors have their ordinary disk topology, their closures away from their boundary are disjoint from $A$, and the omitted closed disks are closed in $Y_*$. They cover because $r_0<r_1$. Each $V_i$ is an open disk, different $V_i$ are disjoint, and their overlaps with $U$ are exactly the annuli $r_0<|v|<r_1$. On each outer collar, increasing its radius by $r\mapsto(1-s)r+s$ retracts $U$ to $A$, fixing $A$. Step 5.1 supplies its meridian basis. Transfer these sets and the composed homotopies back through the finite normalizations in steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1. They give the stated subspace and cover in the original exterior.

For the resulting round circle use $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$, $K=\{z_1=0\}$, and infinity $p=(1,0)$. Choose the angular coordinate so that increasing $t$ gives the positively oriented meridian (replace $t$ by $-t$ if the carried knot orientation requires it). The map $(w,e^{it})\longmapsto(\sqrt{1-|w|^2}e^{it},w)$ identifies $S^3\setminus K$ with $D^\circ\times S^1$, and $p$ with $(0,1)$. Choose a center-preserving homeomorphism from $D^\circ$ to $(-1,1)^2$. For $q\in(-1,1)^2$, put $r=\|q\|_\infty$ and define
$$c(q)=\begin{cases}q,&r\le\tfrac12,\\[2pt]q/(2r),&r>\tfrac12.\end{cases}$$
The homotopy $C_s(q)=(1-s)q+sc(q)$ stays in the open square, fixes $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]^2$, and preserves $q=0$. Therefore $(q,z)\mapsto(C_s(q),z)$ is a strong deformation retraction of $(D^\circ\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$ onto $([-1/2,1/2]^2\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$: when $z=1$, every point in the punctured fiber has $q\ne0$, and $C_s(q)$ is a positive scalar multiple of $q$, so the homotopy never reaches the puncture. Rescaling the square gives $([-1,1]^2\times S^1)\setminus\{(0,1)\}$. Write $S^1=[-1,1]/(-1\sim1)$ with the puncture at circle coordinate $0$. For $v\in[-1,1]^3\setminus\{0\}$, the homotopy
$$H_s(v)=\left(1-s+\frac{s}{\|v\|_\infty}\right)v$$
retracts onto the cube boundary, fixes both identified end faces pointwise, and therefore descends to the product quotient. Its image $X_0$ is a finite CW complex: the lateral faces form the torus $T=\partial[-1,1]^2\times S^1$, and the two square end faces become one disk $D^2$ attached along $\ell=\partial[-1,1]^2\times\{1\}$. Give $T$ its product CW structure with $\ell$ as a subcomplex; then $D^2$ is a contractible CW subcomplex of $X_0$. By [F4], collapsing it is a homotopy equivalence, and the quotient is $T$ with $\ell$ collapsed. Cutting $T$ along $\ell$ gives a cylinder; after the two boundary copies of $\ell$ are collapsed to their common point, the quotient is a sphere with its two poles identified.

To identify its homotopy type explicitly, let $Z$ be $S^2$ with an interval attached at its two distinct poles. Give $Z$ the finite CW structure in which the interval is a 1-cell and its endpoints are 0-cells, so the interval is a contractible subcomplex. Collapsing it identifies the poles, so [F4] makes $Z$ homotopy equivalent to the sphere-with-poles-identified quotient. The two endpoint maps of the interval into $S^2$ are homotopic along a fixed path; choose this path to be the $e^{it}$ meridian cut at $t=0$. By the attaching-map clause of [F3], $Z$ is homotopy equivalent to the adjunction space with both endpoints attached at one pole, namely $S^2\vee S^1$, and the new circle is the retained positive meridian.

For this wedge with wedge point $w$, choose $q\in S^2\setminus\{w\}$ and $r\in S^1\setminus\{w\}$, and set
$$A=S^1\cup(S^2\setminus\{q\}),\qquad B'=(S^1\setminus\{r\})\cup S^2.$$
These are open in the wedge topology and cover $S^1\vee S^2$. The first deformation retracts to $S^1$, the second to $S^2$, so both are path-connected; their overlap $(S^1\setminus\{r\})\cup(S^2\setminus\{q\})$ is nonempty and contracts to $w$ by contracting each punctured summand to $w$. Thus the sets and overlap satisfy the path-connected open-cover hypotheses of van Kampen [F5], which gives $\pi_1(S^1\vee S^2,w)\cong\pi_1(S^1,w)*\pi_1(S^2,w)\cong\mathbb Z*1\cong\mathbb Z$, generated by the positive meridian circle. Finally the normal radial homotopy [F2] proves the asserted retraction onto $E_K$ in every case.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a regular diagram represented by a valid finite planar code, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. Choose a sufficiently small closed normal tube $N(K)$ and set $E_K=\mathbb R^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. If $c>0$, there is a subspace $Y\subset E_K$, fixed pointwise by a strong deformation retraction of $E_K$, with a finite relative-open cover
$$Y=U\cup V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_c.$$
The space $U$ deformation retracts to a wedge of $c$ circles. With a common basepoint in the collar above the diagram and access paths in that collar extended into the arc charts, the positive under-arc meridians are its free basis. Each $V_i$ is contractible, $U\cap V_i$ is an open annulus around the $i$-th crossing attachment, and distinct $V_i$ are disjoint. Thus $V_i$ meets $U$ and any previously attached crossing pieces precisely in $U\cap V_i$.

For $c=0$, the Euclidean complement has homotopy type $S^1\vee S^2$, with the circle represented by the positive meridian. In particular its fundamental group is infinite cyclic; the extra sphere at infinity must not be discarded. In all cases the punctured normal tube retracts radially to its boundary, giving a strong deformation retraction $\mathbb R^3\setminus K\to E_K$. These constructions require only finitely many charts and no choice axiom.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

A topological space $X$ is **simply connected** when it is nonempty and
path-connected ([[def-path-connected]]) and, for every $x_0\in X$, the group
$\pi_1(X,x_0)$ has exactly one element.

Requiring every basepoint avoids presuming a change-of-basepoint theorem. For a
path-connected space that later theorem shows that checking one basepoint is
equivalent, but no such result is needed for this definition. The empty space
is path-connected under the published convention, but it is not simply
connected here because nonemptiness is explicit.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-seifert-van-kampen]], if $U\cap V$ is simply connected, then the inclusion-induced homomorphisms give an isomorphism

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)*\pi_1(V,x_0)\cong\pi_1(X,x_0).$$

Let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous and let $x_0\in X$. Composition sends a loop
$\alpha$ at $x_0$ to the loop $f\circ\alpha$ at $f(x_0)$. Using the loop
classes and fundamental group of [[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]],
the proposed
**induced homomorphism** is

$$f_*:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(Y,f(x_0)),\qquad f_*([\alpha]):=[f\circ\alpha].$$

The next theorem proves that this value is independent of the representative,
that it is a group homomorphism in the sense of [[def-group-homomorphism]], and
that induced maps respect identities, composition and homotopies that fix the
basepoint.

Let $f:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ be a continuous map with $f(x_0)=y_0$. Then

$$f_*([\alpha])=[f\circ\alpha]$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism. For pointed continuous maps,

$$\operatorname{id}_*=\operatorname{id},\qquad (g\circ f)_*=g_*\circ f_*.$$

If $f_0,f_1:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ are homotopic through a homotopy that keeps
$x_0$ at $y_0$, then $(f_0)_*=(f_1)_*$.

For every pointed topological space $(X,x_0)$, the product

$$[\alpha][\beta]=[\alpha*\beta]$$

is well defined and makes $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ a group. Its identity is the class of
the constant loop $c_{x_0}$, and $[\alpha]^{-1}=[\bar\alpha]$.

Since $K$ is compact, choose $R>0$ with $K$ and $b$ in the open ball $D=B_R(0)$. Put $U=S^3\setminus(K\cup\{\infty\})=\mathbb R^3\setminus K$ and $V=S^3\setminus\overline D$. Then $V$ is an open ball about infinity, disjoint from $K$, and $U\cap V=V\setminus\{\infty\}$. First verify that $U$ is path-connected without assuming a diagram code. Parameterize the smooth embedded circle by $k:S^1\to K$. For $p\in U$, the cone
$$C_p=\{p+t(k(s)-p):s\in S^1,\ t\ge1\}$$
has three-dimensional outer volume zero: on each of finitely many smooth coordinate intervals of $S^1$ and each bounded interval $1\le t\le n$, the defining map is Lipschitz on a compact rectangle; subdividing into $O(N^2)$ squares of side $1/N$ covers its image by balls of radius $O(1/N)$, whose total three-dimensional volume is $O(1/N)$. Thus each truncated image has outer volume zero, and the countable union over $n$ does also. Given $p,q\in U$, choose $r$ in an open ball outside $C_p\cup C_q$, which is possible because that union has outer volume zero. If the segment $[p,r]$ met $K$ at $k(s)$, then $r=p+t(k(s)-p)$ for some $t\ge1$, contrary to $r\notin C_p$; similarly $[q,r]$ misses $K$. The broken line from $p$ to $r$ to $q$ lies in $U$.

Under inversion $J(x)=x/\|x\|^2$, extended by $J(\infty)=0$, the set $V$ is the open ball of radius $1/R$ about $0$. The radial homotopy $y\mapsto(1-t)y$ contracts it to $0$, so it is nonempty and path-connected. Since this ball is convex, every based loop contracts to its own basepoint by the straight-line homotopy inside the ball; [F3] therefore makes $V$ simply connected. The same inversion identifies $U\cap V$ with $0<\|y\|<1/R$. Fix $\rho=1/(2R)$; the puncture-preserving radial homotopy
$$y\longmapsto\left((1-t)+t\frac{\rho}{\|y\|}\right)y$$
is a strong deformation retraction of this punctured ball onto the sphere $S^2_\rho$. The punctured ball is path-connected. For any basepoint $y$ in it, let $i:S^2_\rho\hookrightarrow U\cap V$ be inclusion and let $r$ be the radial retraction. Then $r_*i_*$ is the identity, while $i_*r_*$ is an isomorphism: the radial deformation from $\operatorname{id}$ to $i r$ has a basepoint track, and [F7, F8] identify its induced map with the corresponding basepoint-change isomorphism. Hence $r_*$ is an isomorphism. Scaling identifies $S^2_\rho$ with $S^2$, which is simply connected at every basepoint by [F2]; thus [F3] makes $U\cap V$ simply connected.

Choose $b_0\in U\cap V$. The open sets $U,V$ cover $S^3\setminus K$; [F4] applies by the path-connectedness in step 1.1. Since $V$ and $U\cap V$ are simply connected by step 1.1, the special case [F5] shows that inclusion induces an isomorphism $\pi_1(U,b_0)\to\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b_0)$.

The inclusion induces the based map by [F6]. A path in $U$ from $b$ to $b_0$ exists by step 1.1 and gives basepoint-change isomorphisms by [F8]; functoriality [F7] makes the inclusion square commute. Thus the map at $b$ is also an isomorphism.

classes and fundamental group of [[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]],
the proposed
**induced homomorphism** is

$$f_*:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(Y,f(x_0)),\qquad f_*([\alpha]):=[f\circ\alpha].$$

that it is a group homomorphism in the sense of [[def-group-homomorphism]], and
that induced maps respect identities, composition and homotopies that fix the
basepoint.

Let $f:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ be a continuous map with $f(x_0)=y_0$. Then

$$f_*([\alpha])=[f\circ\alpha]$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism. For pointed continuous maps,

$$\operatorname{id}_*=\operatorname{id},\qquad (g\circ f)_*=g_*\circ f_*.$$

If $f_0,f_1:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ are homotopic through a homotopy that keeps
$x_0$ at $y_0$, then $(f_0)_*=(f_1)_*$.

For every pointed topological space $(X,x_0)$, the product

$$[\alpha][\beta]=[\alpha*\beta]$$

is well defined and makes $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ a group. Its identity is the class of
the constant loop $c_{x_0}$, and $[\alpha]^{-1}=[\bar\alpha]$.
